#9885. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

#9879. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9876. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features

Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9875. AI Doom or AI Bubble? What to Actually Expect from AI in the Next Two Years

If you follow AI news, you’ve probably noticed two stories running side by side. In one, AI is so powerful that it may wipe out humanity within a few years. In the other, AI is wildly overhyped and the money pouring into it is a bubble about to burst. Even Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, has said investors are “overexcited” about AI.

Both stories can’t be fully true at once. Either AI is about to become all-powerful, or it’s a lot less impressive than the valuations suggest. I work with tech companies on content and strategy, and I kept hearing smart people repeat one headline or the other. So I went looking for a more grounded view.

One of the most level-headed takes I came across was from Denis Stebunov, CEO of the software development company ivelum, who recently recorded his thoughts on these headlines. His view, which I’ll lean on throughout this piece, is that the doomsday scenario and the bubble panic both miss what’s actually going on with AI, and what we should expect from it over the next couple of years.

It’s natural to feel uneasy about AI. It’s new, it moves fast, and few people fully understand how it works. Anxiety about the unknown is a very human reaction. But Stebunov argues there’s more to the doomsday narrative than ordinary nerves.

The first factor is old and well documented: bad news sells. Open any news site and the headlines are about wars, hurricanes, crashes, and crimes. Plenty of good things happen too; they just don’t get the clicks. “Bad news drive more engagement,” as Stebunov puts it. “People are more likely to click on something that sparks anxiety.” A study published in Nature Human Behaviour analyzed about 105,000 headline variations tested on the news site Upworthy and found that each additional negative word in a headline raised the click-through rate by about 2.3%.

The second factor is less obvious. The warnings about AI’s dangers don’t only come from random people online. They come from the leading AI companies, which talk to the public and to governments about risks and regulation. In Stebunov’s view, raising these concerns has become part of the PR strategy of the two largest AI labs, OpenAI and Anthropic. A product that might be dangerous is, by implication, a very powerful product. “It’s a bold move,” he says, “and it’s clearly working.”

The third factor is cultural. Most of us grew up on The Terminator and The Matrix, which paint a vivid picture of machines taking over. More hopeful visions exist, Star Trek among them, but they don’t stick the same way. So when someone mentions very advanced AI, most people picture Skynet, a story they already know.

None of this means AI is harmless. Stebunov has concerns of his own, and the most concrete is cybersecurity.

The threat is no longer hypothetical. In November 2025, Anthropic reported that it had disrupted a cyber-espionage campaign by a state-sponsored group that used its AI model to attack roughly 30 organizations. The AI carried out 80 to 90% of the tactical work on its own, according to the report, with humans stepping in mainly to approve the big decisions.

But the same technology works on defense. In July 2025, Google said its AI agent Big Sleep had found a critical vulnerability in SQLite, a widely used open-source database, that attackers were preparing to exploit. Google called it the first time an AI agent had directly foiled an exploitation attempt in the wild.

“It’s more like a cat-and-mouse game,” Stebunov says, “which probably will be accelerating.” Attackers get faster, defenders get faster, and organizations that don’t keep up will pay for it. That’s a serious problem, and a very different one from the end of humanity.

In fairness, the doomsayers are mostly not talking about today’s AI. They mean future systems that will be far more capable, and their argument goes: look how much progress AI made in the past few years, and imagine where it will be in a few more.

“This is a classic extrapolation,” Stebunov says. You take the past trend and assume it will continue at the same pace, or faster. That’s a reasonable starting point, but only if you understand where the past progress came from.

The technology behind today’s chatbots goes back to 2017, when researchers at Google introduced the transformer architecture. In 2018, OpenAI built on it with GPT, the generative pre-trained transformer. That was the scientific breakthrough.

What followed, in Stebunov’s words, was “not a series of scientific breakthroughs, but rather scaling of the same idea.” The industry discovered that the bigger the model and the more it’s trained, the better it performs. That’s where most of the money went: bigger models, more compute, more data centers.

There were also two important advances in how the models are used. First, they learned to use tools. Second came agents, which run the model in a loop with the right tools and context so it can work through a task step by step. “That was big,” Stebunov says. “Agents can now perform real tasks, and this has already changed how people work.”

Still, the research itself produced no new fundamental breakthrough. Ilya Sutskever, one of OpenAI’s co-founders, has made the same point. He has described 2012 to 2020 as the age of research and 2020 to 2025 as the age of scaling, and argued that making models a hundred times bigger won’t transform everything. In his view, the field is heading back to research.

If most recent progress came from scaling, the question is how long scaling can continue. Not forever, Stebunov says, though nobody knows when it will slow down. “Maybe it will plateau in the next year, or maybe not.”

A genuine new breakthrough would change the picture, and he isn’t aware of one on the horizon. Without it, his forecast is refreshingly unexciting: “We’ll probably have more or less the same, just better, and with more practical applications.”

In practice, that means steady improvement rather than leaps: models that keep getting better at reasoning, coding, and following instructions. The biggest gains will come from putting the existing models to work in narrow, well-defined areas where agents can handle real tasks. And much of the change will come from more companies figuring out how to use what already exists, rather than from smarter models arriving.

That’s a long way from superintelligence by 2028, and a long way from a technology about to collapse.

The bubble worry isn’t made up. In August 2025, Sam Altman told reporters: “Are we in a phase where investors as a whole are overexcited about AI? My opinion is yes.”

The numbers explain the nerves. According to Futurum Group, the five largest US cloud and AI infrastructure companies planned to spend roughly $660 to $690 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, nearly double the year before. OpenAI ended 2025 with about $20 billion in annualized revenue, and Futurum estimated that all pure-play AI vendors together would bring in under $35 billion in 2026, a small fraction of what’s going into infrastructure.

So a correction is entirely possible. But a bubble is about valuations and expectations, not about whether the underlying technology is useful. The dot-com crash is the obvious comparison. When it hit in 2000, the Nasdaq lost most of its value and many companies disappeared. The internet didn’t. It went on to reshape almost every industry, and some of the survivors became the giants of today.

Stebunov makes a similar point about AI. OpenAI and Anthropic may have the best technology today, but they’re far from the only players: there are open-weight Chinese models, Mistral in Europe, Google, xAI, and others. Even if some of the most expensive bets fail, the models already exist, and many of them can be downloaded and run by anyone. “The technology proved its usefulness,” he says. “It is here to stay.”

If neither the apocalypse nor the crash is the main story, what is? For Stebunov, the answer is work, and his own industry is in the front line. “While I don’t believe that AI will wipe out humanity,” he says, “I think it may wipe out some jobs, particularly in the software development industry.” And that will happen whether or not the bubble bursts.

That’s where the conversation about AI is worth having: which tasks AI takes over, which skills become more valuable, and how companies should adapt.

Stebunov describes himself as fairly optimistic about AI, and after looking into it, so am I. We have a remarkable new technology that, like every technology before it, can be used for good and for harm. The risks are real, but they’re specific and manageable, and they look nothing like the movies.

The bubble may or may not burst. Either way, AI will keep improving step by step and finding its way into more of the work we do. That’s less thrilling than the headlines and more useful to plan for.

As Stebunov puts it: “We humans are extremely adaptable. We survived the ice age, and I’m sure we’ll figure out how to deal with AI.”

The Model Is the Easy Part: What Actually Breaks When AI Goes to Production

#9874. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9870. nemotron-halloween

TL;DR: MonsterHouse is an interactive projection I created for Halloween. He listens to trick-or-treaters, answers in the voice of a grumpy old pirate ship and softens when visitors remember their manners. He is built on the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent with NVIDIA Nemotron ASR, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, Magpie TTS Zeroshot and Audio2Face-3D, and he runs on a single workstation.

I wanted the kids visiting my house at Halloween to interact in a fun and unique way. The house was going to be in charge and giving out the treats, but more grumpy than scary. Somehow, my solution was to give the garage door a mouth and teach him to complain.

That became MonsterHouse: a grumpy old building with pirate stories, a fiery grin and a suspicious weakness for “please.” NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent supplies the conversation foundation. Nemotron Speech does the listening, Bolt E4B is the brain, NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot is the live voice, and NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D makes the wooden mouth talk.

The mouth came first. I imagined the wooden garage door boards splitting into jagged lips, with the burning flames of hell illuminating the driveway from beyond whenever he opened his cursed mouth. He needed to look ancient, expressive and mildly offended by the existence of visitors.

A few expressions from a house with plenty to say.

Creating a custom animation rig was one of the more labor intensive parts of the build. After bashing it into submission, I could export the facial expression shapes that Audio2Face-3D could later animate. The character SkelMesh was built in Autodesk Maya then exported into Unreal Engine where virtual fire and effects were added behind the door. With no eyes, no eyebrows and no blinking, he’s a surprisingly economical monster.

While all the nonsense of building the character was going on, NVIDIA built the Nemotron Voice Agent. What was supposed to be the hard part of the build now became rather fun, iterative and easy. I had a foundation for listening, conversation and speech right out of the box. The house already had a mouth. Now he could finally find something to complain about.

The house needed a past as cantankerous as its personality so I devised a backstory that the house had been built from the timbers of a sunken pirate ship, haunted by its stormy past. The nautical complaints now had a reason. This was the ship, reincarnated as real estate and not entirely pleased about it.

The performance needed a guide, a path to follow from greeting to goodbye while providing treats along the way. First, the house would brush visitors off with remarks like “I’m busy grumbling, go bother the neighbors!” But persistence would wear him down. A “Please” could break through immediately, and “thank you” earned a warm farewell. Once a visitor won him over, I wanted him to stay won over. Nobody wants to negotiate with the same garage door twice.

Here is where the Voice Agent really shines. You can choose any LLM you like. Because I wanted the system to be off-grid and completely self-contained, I had a memory and compute budget.

The character needs more than a prompt that says “be grumpy.” It had to follow a master conversation flow, respond to what visitors actually said, track encounter state, and leave enough compute for the rest of the pipeline.

After testing more than a dozen models, I landed on Bolt E4B to supply the live dialogue. It is an open small language model purpose-built for local conversational agents and interactive characters, which is a fair description of a talking garage door. I use the 4-bit quantized release (the “4GB” in its name) as the default response model, with the BF16 checkpoint available for comparison.

If it’s not obvious by now, I work at NVIDIA and due to this I was able to test Bolt E4B before its public release and found it to be a solid choice, with a smaller footprint than other frontrunners- Qwen3 30B-A3B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B.

It works inside the Nemotron Voice Agent pipeline, turning what visitors say into the next suitably reluctant reply.

Bolt provides the conversational foundation. My prompts, application logic and LoRA adapter trained on thousands of reviewed example conversations shape it into this particular stubborn ship.

Creating a dataset of over 5000 multi-turn conversations meant I could train LoRAs for each model I felt good enough to be an option. Some took about an hour to train, some took a couple. A local agent ran everything and benchmarked the results. That agent and a very large LLM created and judged the dataset to begin with. This happened at night or while I was doing the day job.

With the LoRA in place I check the replies for continuity, timing and tone, benchmark models and adapters for quality, repetition and speed, and then listen to the performance. The house should give in eventually, without turning into a cheerful concierge. A little resistance is part of the charm. An endless argument with a garage door is not.

Two shortcuts, two outputs. Authored text skips fresh dialogue generation, and saved audio skips synthesis. Clean speech drives the animation separately from the audience effects.

A haunted house loses authority if he takes too long to complain. The pipeline releases speakable text before an entire answer is finished, so the house can start talking while the rest of the sentence is still on its way. Prepared greetings and candy jokes cover familiar encounters: the text bank saves language-model work, and cached recordings save speech synthesis. Even an ancient grump benefits from rehearsing.

NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot turns text into the Queen’s English. Its zero-shot voice conditioning uses a short reference sample instead of a trained voice; mine supplies the grumpy pirate character. The house has seven moods, from grumpy and menacing to amused and delighted, and emotion tags dictated by the prompt template and provided by the LLM choose how each line is delivered. Since each emotion requires a different 3-10 second voice sample I added a “Sample your Voice” block on the UI’s tool tab. I could then read and record a sample line of text in my best happy pirate or angry pirate voice. When it’s “Go” time, Bolt E4B decides what to say, and Magpie turns that text into speech with the proper delight or despair.

Next down the pipe is Audio2Face-3D and the 3d character scene I created in Epic’s Unreal Engine. The default model weights work best with a clean neutral male or female voice, not too deep, not too high (choose the appropriate gendered model for your use case). I wanted the house to have a very deep and demonic voice with echo and chamber. In this case, since my voice samples don’t have that theatrical heft, it’s actually a benefit. Audio2Face-3D gets clean speech from the samples and a second audio stream adds adjustable real-time vocal effects that play out the speakers.

To keep everything running smoothly, I split the work to a pair of GPUs: the language and voice model pipeline runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q, and Unreal Engine graphics with Audio2Face-3D runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell. Memory isn’t the issue, compute is. I want to keep animation at a consistent frame rate regardless of what processing the agent pipeline is doing.

Voice, animation and effects have to land together. A convincing monster needs more than a fast answer; it needs to sound as though the complaint belongs to the building. In my case, he does. Tweaks to sync audio delivery are available. I’ve found I could set them and forget them. (100ms compensates for the Audio2Face-3D buffering)

Somewhere along the way, “make the house talk” required an interface full of controls. I can audition cached lines, adjust the opening mood, follow the conversation, change the voice treatment and tune the mouth animation. Tabs cover conversations, model selection, recordings, prompts, performance monitoring and camera feeds, and a soundboard and custom dialogue field let me put words in his mouth. There are also model-loading controls and an Unreal Engine connection indicator, because sometimes the monster is not sulking. He is disconnected.

The MonsterHouse control desk, with the soundboard, custom lines, opening mood and conversation flow.

The fire and glow have joined the act. Editable rules tie visual cues to delivery: live cues begin with speech, while recorded performances can follow a saved timeline. I can direct a change of mood without rebuilding the scene.

Live mode runs the trick-or-treat character. Demo mode persuades The house to explain himself. Microphone mode lets me speak through the house directly, bypassing recognition, dialogue generation and speech synthesis. My clean voice drives the mouth; the audience hears the treated version. The house considers this possession. I consider it a useful fallback.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is a VLM that gives the house visual context. As an optional observer, it interprets camera images and describes visible costumes so the character has something specific to react to. Not looking to reinvent every wheel, I chose the popular object detection and tracking models YOLO and ByteTrack to count and track people currently in view. Keeping those jobs separate lets the house notice a group without asking Omni to narrate every frame.

For a suitably ridiculous test, I gave Omni a video of five costumed sheep at the door. Its saved analysis identified the pirate, vampire, witch, pumpkin and ghost outfits. That is the sort of visual context I want the house to use. Apparently even livestock have more elaborate Halloween plans than I do.

Five very woolly trick-or-treaters in a synthetic test replay. Costume labels come from the saved Omni analysis; boxes and track IDs are illustrative.

The sheep are a synthetic test, not evidence of a successful Halloween night. Real driveway groups, costumes and night lighting still need testing. Detection does trigger automatic greetings, but I fear trendy costume identification and suitably witty retorts may need some post training. Since the house has no eyes, he calls his visitor awareness echolocation. I am letting him have that one.

There is more to do: the animation can always improve, complete performance testing needs real visitors, and candy will one day be provided automatically. I have not yet reached the original goal of leaving him to run Halloween while I head off with my family to see the other neighborhood ghouls. But that is still the point of all this. One day a child will meet a grumpy old house, try a little kindness and discover that the old timber has a soft spot. And gives out candy bars.

The MonsterHouse code itself is not packaged for release, but every NVIDIA model it uses is available today, and the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent gets you most of the way. This is the path I would follow.

A cached response bank and saved audio for your most common lines will make even a slow monster feel quick. In fact, if you happen to be limited by computing power, there is no reason why you can’t have a Live version that just uses Nemotron 3 ASR, a python conversation router, with all cached audio. You can use the Bolt E4B and Magpie pipeline to generate 100s of responses offline, then use the cache for the show. I’ll be doing this for the interactive pumpkins.

#9868. Why LLMs Struggle With Constraint-Based Scheduling and How Optimization Solvers Help

Senior Software Engineer building large-scale financial data systems with distributed systems, AI, and LLMs.

Senior Software Engineer building large-scale financial data systems with distributed systems, AI, and LLMs.

Senior Software Engineer building large-scale financial data systems with distributed systems, AI, and LLMs.

Imagine you are building a two-week staff schedule. The requirements look simple enough:

None of these rules is hard to understand by itself. Then you look at weekend coverage.

Across the four weekend days, the staffing targets ask for 35 employee shifts. But there are 14 employees, and each can work only one weekend, which means at most two weekend days each. Fourteen times two is 28.

Before I assign a single person to a single shift, at least seven weekend slots are already impossible to fill.

This is the part of scheduling that interests me when large language models are involved. A model can understand every requirement correctly and still hand back a schedule that breaks once those requirements start affecting each other. In this article I will show that with a public example, explain why it happens, and lay out how I would split the work between a language model and ordinary software.

To keep it reproducible, I used Instance2 from the University of Nottingham nurse rostering benchmark and rebuilt it as an optimization model. [1] The examples use public benchmark data and general engineering patterns. They do not describe any employer's internal implementation.

Instance2 covers 14 days with 14 employees and two shift types, Early and Late, each eight hours long.

Its rules fall into two groups, and the difference between them turns out to be the whole story.

If staffing coverage were a hard rule too, the weekend numbers alone would make this schedule impossible. No valid answer would exist.

Because coverage is soft, the question changes. It is no longer "can I satisfy everything?" It becomes "what is the best valid schedule when not every goal can be met?"

Fourteen employees, one weekend each, two days in that weekend: 28 possible shifts against 35 requested. The minimum shortage is seven, and that is before I consider days off, who is allowed to work which shift, working-time limits, or the Late-to-Early rule.

The arithmetic is easy. Finding the best schedule once all of those rules start interacting is the hard part.

For this experiment, I rebuilt Instance2 as a mathematical optimization model and solved it with HiGHS, an open-source solver, through the SciPy library in Python. I will skip the equations and describe the idea, because the idea is what matters.

Think of every possible assignment as a yes-or-no switch. "Employee A works the Late shift on day 5" is one switch. With 14 employees, 14 days, and 2 shifts, there are 392 of them. A schedule is simply a choice of which switches are on.

Each hard rule then becomes a restriction on which switches may be on together:

The weekend rule needs one extra step, and it is worth spelling out because it drives the opening example. I add a second kind of switch that says "this employee works this weekend." Turning on any Saturday or Sunday shift forces that weekend switch on. Then the rule is simple: each employee may have at most one weekend switch on.

With that in place, the 35 versus 28 conflict stops being an observation in my introduction. It lives inside the model, where the solver has to respect it.

Coverage is soft, so it gets counters, not locks. For every shift, I track how many people are missing and how many are extra. The number assigned, plus the number missing, minus the number extra, must equal the number required.

Then each kind of miss gets a price. In Instance2:

The solver's job is to find the valid schedule with the lowest total penalty.

This gives the system three things a paragraph of instructions never does: an exact definition of what makes a schedule invalid, a list of what may be traded away, and a price for each trade.

The solver finished with a proven best score of 828.

The public benchmark lists Instance2 with a best-known lower bound of 828 and a best-known solution of 828. When a real schedule reaches the lower bound, nothing better can exist, so 828 is optimal. [1] My rebuilt model landed on the same number, which told me I had reconstructed the problem correctly.

The score breaks down like this: 8 missing staffing assignments at 100 points each makes 800, and employee preference penalties add 28, for a total of 828.

The weekend arithmetic had already proved that at least seven assignments would be missing. Once every other rule was included, the best possible schedule needed eight.

One detail is worth noting. A score of 828 does not point to one unique schedule. Different schedules can spread those eight gaps differently and still score the same. The useful result is that the schedule is valid and the score is proven, not any particular arrangement of names.

Take five of these requirements: Employee D cannot work Late. Employee A must have day 3 off. Late cannot be followed by Early. Each employee can work at most one weekend. Saturday needs ten people.

A language model may understand every one of those statements perfectly. The trouble starts when assignments begin to affect each other:

Every assignment changes the choices that remain. Keeping track of all of that at once is a different skill from reading a rule.

A recent benchmark called SCHEDBench shows the same thing at larger scale. It evaluates 13 language models across 1,132 scheduling problems whose correct answers are backed by a solver. [2] On its nurse rostering problems, the share of model-produced schedules that were valid averaged 97.0% on easy problems, 62.4% on medium ones, and 1.7% on hard ones.

The study also found that models were sensitive to the order in which the rules were presented. The underlying problem stayed exactly the same, yet shuffling the rules changed how often the models broke them.

Another benchmark, R-ConstraintBench, reports a related pattern: validity drops as resource limits, downtime, time windows, and either-or constraints begin to interact. [3]

So the boundary that matters is not whether a model can read a rule. It is whether it can hold the entire valid state in mind while many rules push against each other.

Real scheduling requirements rarely arrive as equations. A manager writes things like:

"Bob can work one weekend, but not both."

"Anyone finishing Late should not open the next morning."

This is where a language model earns its place. It can turn Bob's sentence into a structured rule: the employee is Bob, the rule type is a maximum number of weekends, the value is one, and the window is 14 days.

I would keep these out of the model's hands:

Suppose the original requirement says "Alice must have Saturday off," and the interpretation step records it as a preference instead of a requirement.

The solver will return a mathematically perfect answer to the wrong problem, and Alice will be on the Saturday rota.

For any rule that matters, I would keep three things side by side:

A solver can only guarantee what it was given. The translation into rules still needs a human or a separate check to sign it off.

I would also check the finished schedule outside the solver. Useful checks include:

By independent checking, I do not mean running the same model twice. Where practical, the checks should be written separately from the model, so a mistake made while building the model is less likely to appear in both places.

A solver, an interpretation layer, and an independent checker all add complexity. They should earn it.

If you are putting a language model anywhere near scheduling, rostering, or planning, here is what I would do:

The first useful result appeared before the solver ever ran: 35 weekend shifts requested, 28 possible under the weekend rule, at least 7 gaps unavoidable. The full model needed 8 gaps and produced a proven best score of 828.

Every individual requirement was easy to read. The difficult part was making them all hold at once.

That is the boundary I would protect in any LLM-assisted scheduling system. Let the language model help interpret messy requirements. Once those requirements become precise rules, let deterministic software search for the schedule and verify it.

A schedule can look reasonable and still break a rule somewhere you were not looking. In any system with this many interacting rules, validity has to be checked, never assumed.

[1] University of Nottingham, Nurse Rostering Benchmark Instances, including the raw data for Instance2 and its published optimal score of 828.

[2] Shrenil Shaun Sharma and Avi Sharma, “SCHEDBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Constraint Faithfulness in Natural-Language Combinatorial Scheduling,” arXiv:2608.00991 (2026).

[3] Raj Jain and Marc Wetter, “R-ConstraintBench: Evaluating LLMs on NP-Complete Scheduling,” arXiv:2508.15204 (2025).

#9864. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9863. The CFO Who Learned to Code by Shipping: How I Use Hackathons to Keep Up With AI Tools

AI and Blockchain developer with domain focus on Corporate finance and supply chain applications

AI and Blockchain developer with domain focus on Corporate finance and supply chain applications

AI and Blockchain developer with domain focus on Corporate finance and supply chain applications

Oh hey. I'm Shyam Desigan (most people call me Sam). I spent twenty-plus years in finance, mostly as a CFO. Now I'm a Director of Technology Consulting, and I learn the tech stack by building real things with AI tools, usually against a hackathon deadline.

I'm Director, Technology Consulting at Tiger Analytics in New York. I moved into the role in September 2026 after a long career in finance leadership. Outside the day job, I build. Since February 2026 I've submitted more than 35 projects to hackathons on Devpost, plus a steady stream on DoraHacks, lablab.ai and others. My favorite part is that these two halves feed each other. A business problem I understand from years of running finance becomes something I can actually prototype, and every build teaches me a tool or a layer of the stack I'd otherwise only read about.

Honestly, I came in through the finance door. After my MBA at Indiana University's Kelley School of Business, I spent my career in finance. My first official tech title came at the American Academy of Physician Associates, where I was CFO and Senior VP of IT, so the systems and the books were both my job. After that came KIC Ventures, Sproxil, TechCXO, Purim Ventures, BlackTeal Energy and Green Li-ion, and every role pulled me further into data, automation and systems. What changed recently is that AI tools made it realistic for someone like me to build software, not just spec it. My first hackathon submission I can find is a Commodity Price Analyzer for the Airia AI Agents Hackathon in February 2026. Within a few months I had won a prize at DeveloperWeek New York and an award at Mantle's Turing Test Hackathon, and that convinced me the approach worked.

Green, but the green of a runway dashboard, not a flag. In my world green means the cash lasts past the next milestone, the risks are known and nobody is panicking. A utopia would be a place where most people's "status light" is green: enough runway to try things, fail and try again. That's also the setup I'm trying to give myself as a learner.

I'll take the second one. My favorite thing is reading builder write-ups by people who explain what broke and how they fixed it, not just what they launched. That kind of honest postmortem has taught me more than most polished tutorials. As a newcomer to building, it helps to see that experienced engineers also hit dead ends, file bug reports and work around flaky tooling. HackerNoon has also been part of my building directly. My project CHP Locknet was shortlisted for the Decentralized Compute Track of the HackerNoon × Nosana Decentralized AI Hackathon. I'd like this interview to be my first contribution in the write-up spirit.

I treat hackathons as a forced curriculum. Each one drops me into a different tool and a different layer of the stack, with a deadline that keeps me honest. These are the builds I'm proudest of:

I don't do this alone. I work with a small team of AI agents (assistant bots) that handle research and parts of the builds, and our code lives under the GitHub org icohangar-ops. I act as the CFO of that team as much as its developer. I decide what's worth building, check the output and own the result. I also run on hackathon and startup credits instead of cash, so I'm spending time, not budget, while I learn.

Anyone can show up and contribute. A finance guy can open a pull request on an open-source project, and if the code is right and CI is green, it gets reviewed on the merits. Hackathons work the same way. Nobody asks for your résumé, they look at your demo. That openness is the whole reason my learning plan works.

A solar-charged laptop loaded with offline models and documentation. A laptop is a workshop, a library and a ledger in one box, and with a local model it's also a patient tutor that doesn't need the cloud. Someone would still need to track the group's supplies, and old habits die hard, so I'd probably build the zombie-era runway dashboard on day one.

The noise, especially in finance and crypto, where confident-sounding promises are everywhere and proof is rare. I've learned to trust things I can reproduce: a running app, a passing test, a bug report someone else can follow step by step. That's partly why the ChainSight AI award meant so much to me. It was for a deployment that actually runs, not a slide. The internet rewards loud claims too often. I'd rather be the person who ships the small working thing.

I'd put it into the unglamorous plumbing of critical minerals: recycling, traceability and the financial infrastructure that helps smaller mining companies get to production. I worked on battery recycling at Green Li-ion, building data and systems for commodity pricing and traceability. I've also built hackathon tools in this space, including CritMin Compass and Mineral Watch Agent. Again and again, good projects stall because of capital access and poor data, not geology. I'd pair the capital with agentic tools for diligence and reporting, so smaller companies can look as investable as they really are.

Right now it's agent engineering for real: guardrails, evaluation and running autonomous systems that touch real money and real data. ChainSight AI taught me how much work goes into trusting an alert. Council taught me that several agents checking each other beats one confident agent. Once agents can act, the interesting question is what stops them from acting badly. I'm also learning the parts of the stack I used to hand off, like infrastructure, CI, GPU compute and on-chain plumbing. Each hackathon adds one more layer, and that steady pace matters more to me than any single project.

The future. Ten years ago I would have needed a full engineering team to build what I can now prototype in an afternoon, and I don't want to give that up. I'm curious whether finance work, which still runs on email, data rooms and spreadsheets, will look completely different by then. Part of me wants to go check whether the things I'm building now turned out to matter.

Practical and grateful, with a CFO's skepticism built in. AI didn't make me an engineer overnight. It gave me a fast enough feedback loop that I could become a builder by shipping, breaking things and fixing them in public. Most of my hackathon entries didn't win, and that's fine, because the two that did came out of everything the others taught me. The catch is that AI output is a first draft, not a finished product. Someone still has to read the code, test the edge cases and take responsibility for the result, just like signing off on a set of financials. My advice to other non-engineers is simple: pick a real problem you understand, enter a hackathon with a deadline and let the tools teach you the stack one layer at a time.

#9861. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9860. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.
