#9833. Your Startup's Biggest Security Vulnerability Isn't Your Code — It's You

25+ year entrepreneur, real estate investor & M&A/turnaround specialist. Bestselling author of "The Influence of Military Strategies to Busi

25+ year entrepreneur, real estate investor & M&A/turnaround specialist. Bestselling author of "The Influence of Military Strategies to Busi

25+ year entrepreneur, real estate investor & M&A/turnaround specialist. Bestselling author of "The Influence of Military Strategies to Busi

Alright folks, I’m going to tell you something your dev team already knows but is too polite to say to your face: the biggest security hole in your company isn’t in your codebase. It’s sitting in the founder’s chair.

I’ve spent 25+ years in business warfare — buying troubled companies, turning them around, doing private security consulting, and researching cybersecurity from the operator’s side, not the engineer’s. And I can tell you this with total confidence: when small businesses get hacked, it’s almost never some hoodie-wearing genius cracking encryption. It’s a founder reusing a password. It’s an admin clicking a link. It’s someone handing over the keys because the “IT guy” on the phone sounded convincing.

Here’s the part that should scare you straight. The average cost of a data breach for a small business runs into six figures — and a huge percentage of small businesses that suffer a major breach shut down within months. Not because the hack was sophisticated. Because the recovery was impossible.

Think about it like a military campaign. You’ve built this beautiful fortress — your product, your customer list, your payment systems. And then you leave the back gate open with a sign that says “come on in.” That’s what a reused password is. That’s what an unpatched laptop is. That’s what your executive assistant’s inbox is when nobody’s trained her what a spear-phishing email looks like.

The attackers know this. They’re not wasting zero-days on your seed-stage SaaS. They’re running the cheapest playbook in the book: find the human, fool the human, own the human.

After decades of watching businesses get hit, the pattern is always the same. Different companies, different industries, same five failures:

1. Password reuse across everything. Your founder uses the same password for the company AWS account and some forum he joined in 2019. That forum gets breached, the credentials get sold, and now someone’s logging into your infrastructure at 3 AM. One password, total compromise. This is the single most common way in, and it takes ten minutes to fix with a password manager.

2. No multi-factor authentication on the crown jewels. Email, banking, cloud infrastructure, domain registrar — if these don’t have MFA, you’re one phished password away from losing the company. Your domain registrar alone: if an attacker takes your domain, they own your email, your password resets, everything.

3. Nobody trained the team. Your people are your perimeter. One well-crafted email pretending to be you, asking your bookkeeper to “wire this quickly before the call,” and the money’s gone. I’ve seen it happen to companies with real revenue and real investors. The fix isn’t a $50,000 security audit — it’s a 30-minute training and a culture where nobody wires money on an email request. Ever.

4. The founder’s personal accounts are the backdoor. Here’s the espionage angle: attackers don’t target your company directly. They target you. Your personal email, your social media, your kid’s school portal — anything that can be used for leverage, impersonation, or password-reset chains. If your personal Gmail is the recovery email for your business accounts, your personal security IS your business security.

5. No incident plan. When — not if — something happens, the first hour decides everything. Most founders have no plan: no idea who to call, no backups verified, no idea which accounts to lock down first. Panic is not a strategy. A one-page incident plan written on a calm Tuesday beats a brilliant response improvised during a breach.

Here’s where my background kicks in. In military doctrine, you don’t defend everywhere equally — you defend what matters, and you think like the enemy.

Ask yourself: if I were trying to rob my own company, how would I do it? You’d go after the email first (it’s the master key to every password reset). Then the money (banking, payment processors). Then the customers (their data is your liability). Work backward from there and harden in that order.

This is threat modeling, and you don’t need to be technical to do it. You need to be honest. Most founders aren’t.

You don’t need a security team. You need discipline on the basics — the boring stuff that stops 90% of attacks:

None of this requires an engineer. All of it requires a founder who takes security personally — because the attacker already does.

Cybersecurity isn’t an IT problem for founders. It’s a leadership problem. Your company will never be more secure than your own habits, because you hold the keys to everything.

The good news? The basics work. The attackers are lazy — they’re going after the companies that left the gate open. Close the gate, lock it properly, and they’ll move on to someone easier. That’s not paranoia. That’s just good business warfare.

Want the full field manual? I put together a free 20-Point Cyber Hygiene Checklist — the exact basics above, expanded into a one-page audit you can run on your company this afternoon: https://therealmdwhite.gumroad.com/l/iokmxh

And if you want the complete playbook — threat modeling, incident response plans, vendor security, the works — my Cybersecurity for Non-Technical Founders guide covers it: https://therealmdwhite.gumroad.com/l/ccalsf

#9831. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

Note: This article contains affiliate links, meaning we make a small commission if you buy any premium plan from our link.

#9830. Lovable Alternatives: 7 Options Compared (and When to Switch to Custom Code)

Posted on Nov 4 • Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev

Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev.

The best Lovable alternatives in late 2026 are Bolt, Replit, v0, Base44, Cursor and Claude Code, plus the option most comparison lists skip: moving to custom code with a developer. Which one fits depends less on the AI model underneath and more on three questions: can you get your code out, who owns the backend, and how far from production you are.

I take over and fix apps built with these tools, so this comparison focuses on what matters after the demo works. Pricing below was checked on each vendor's own pricing page in November 2026, except where I say otherwise.

Lovable is good at getting a polished React frontend on screen fast. The reasons founders start shopping around are usually the same few:

If one of these is your reason, it should drive your choice. Switching tools to fix a problem the new tool also has is a common and expensive mistake.

The first four are app builders: you describe what you want and they produce and host an app. The next two are AI coding tools: they work on a codebase you or a developer control. The last is a different decision altogether.

Bolt is the closest match to Lovable in how it feels. You chat, it builds, and it runs the app in the browser. Its backend story is Bolt Cloud, which the homepage describes as covering hosting, databases and user authentication.

On pricing, Bolt's free tier gives 1M tokens a month with a 300K daily cap and Bolt branding on sites. Pro is $25 a month for 10M tokens with rollover, a custom domain and no branding. Teams is $30 per member per month. Bolt bills by tokens rather than credits, which some people find easier to predict, but large projects still use a lot of them because the model has to read more code each time. The original bolt.new codebase is public on GitHub under the MIT license, which is a good sign for transparency, even though the hosted product has moved well past it.

Pick Bolt if you want the Lovable experience with a different pricing model, and your app is still at the prototype stage.

Replit is a full development environment with an AI agent on top. Its homepage lists authentication, a database, hosting and monitoring as built-in services, which makes it the strongest "everything in one place" option on this list.

The Core plan is $20 a month ($18 billed yearly) and Pro is $100 a month ($90 yearly), with higher usage tiers above that. Because Replit gives you an actual workspace with files and a terminal, it is easier for a developer to step in later than with tools that hide the code. I compared it with Lovable in more detail in Lovable vs Replit vs Bolt vs Cursor.

Pick Replit if you want the agent to handle backend logic too, and you like the idea of hosting staying in one place.

v0 is Vercel's AI builder. It is strongest on interface work: pages, components and layouts that look production-grade. It fits teams already planning to host on Vercel. For anything beyond the UI, you connect your own database and auth.

I could not reach v0's pricing page from my research environment this month, and third-party guides disagree about which plans still exist after changes earlier in 2026, so check v0.app/pricing directly rather than trusting a number from a blog (including this one).

Pick v0 if your main pain with Lovable is design quality, and you have, or will hire, someone to build the backend.

Base44 targets non-technical builders making internal tools, dashboards and simple customer-facing apps, with a managed backend included. It is easy to start with, but the trade-off is portability. Third-party pricing guides report that code export and GitHub sync are limited to its higher paid tiers, and that the backend stays tied to Base44's own SDK. I could not confirm this on Base44's official site this month, so verify it before you build anything you might want to move.

Pick Base44 if the app is internal, low-risk, and you are fine with it living on the platform long term.

These two are not app builders. They are what you move to when you want AI help but also want a normal codebase in a normal Git repository.

Cursor is an AI-first code editor. You open your project, and the AI can read the whole codebase, suggest changes across files and run agent tasks. Cursor's pricing page in November 2026 lists a free tier and paid plans at $8, $30, $100 and $200 a month, with third-party model usage billed separately. Its plan lineup has changed several times this year, so treat any older comparison with caution.

Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool. According to its documentation it runs in the terminal, in VS Code and JetBrains, as a desktop app and in the browser. It reads a codebase, edits files, runs commands, and works directly with Git to create branches, commits and pull requests. It needs a Claude subscription or an Anthropic Console account.

Both tools make an experienced developer much faster. Neither turns a non-developer into one. If you export a Lovable app into Cursor or Claude Code without knowing how to review a database migration or an access policy, you have swapped one set of blind spots for another. A sensible pattern is: the founder keeps using a builder for experiments, and a developer uses an AI coding tool on the production repo.

This is the decision that matters most, and it is rarely about which AI tool is "better". Switching makes sense when your app has crossed from prototype into product. Signs you are there:

Custom code does not mean starting over. In many AI-built apps, the UI and the data model are worth keeping. The work is usually hardening: locking down database access, moving secrets server-side, adding proper error handling and logging, setting up a real deployment pipeline, and fixing the parts that only worked in the happy path.

Before you switch tools: Connect your current project to GitHub and export your database first. Whatever you decide next, owning a copy of your code and data keeps every option open.

Use this before you pay for another tool:

If you answer "no" or "not sure" to the first four, fix that before switching anything. If you answer "yes" to the middle two and "no" to the last one, a builder alone is no longer enough.

For a prototype or an idea you are testing, any of the builders above is great value compared with paying for custom development, and the right one is mostly a matter of taste and pricing model. For an app with users and revenue, the tool matters far less than having someone accountable for the code.

If you are at that point, my AI app to production service takes apps built with Lovable, Bolt or Replit and makes them secure, maintainable and ready to scale, without throwing away the work you have already done. If you are not sure how bad things are yet, a production audit is a lower-commitment first step.

I'm Muhammad Moiz, a full-stack developer who builds web apps, SaaS and POS systems, and takes AI-built apps (Lovable, Bolt, Replit) to production. Get in touch.

#9829. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

#9827. Dyslexia Testing Sydney: Why Developers Should Understand Neurodiversity When Designing Digital Experiences

Digital accessibility has become an essential consideration in modern web development. Developers regularly think about colour contrast, screen reader compatibility, keyboard navigation and responsive layouts. However, one important aspect of accessibility is sometimes overlooked: how people with different learning and cognitive needs interact with digital content.

For individuals with dyslexia, navigating websites, reading lengthy articles, completing online forms and using educational platforms may present challenges that traditional accessibility testing does not always identify.

As conversations around dyslexia testing services and learning support continue to develop, there is also an opportunity for technology professionals to better understand how reading differences influence digital experiences.

By recognising the relationship between neurodiversity and accessible design, developers may create websites and applications that are easier to navigate, understand and use for a wider audience.

Dyslexia is a specific learning difficulty that primarily affects accurate and fluent word reading and spelling. It is not associated with low intelligence, poor motivation or a lack of effort.

People with dyslexia may experience difficulties with recognising written words, decoding unfamiliar vocabulary, spelling accurately or reading fluently. These challenges vary between individuals and may become more noticeable when users encounter unfamiliar or complicated written information.

In digital environments, these differences are particularly relevant because so many online activities depend on reading.

From navigating government websites to completing online courses, users frequently encounter interfaces that assume everyone processes written information in similar ways.

Understanding dyslexia allows developers to question those assumptions and consider how digital design may better accommodate different reading needs.

Imagine visiting a website with lengthy paragraphs, unfamiliar terminology, inconsistent navigation and complicated instructions.

For many users, this experience would be frustrating. For someone who experiences reading difficulties, those barriers may become even more significant.

These challenges do not affect every person with dyslexia in the same way. Some individuals may prefer audio content, while others benefit from adjustable text presentation, simplified instructions or greater control over reading speed.

The DEV Community article Challenges and Solutions for People With Disabilities provides additional discussion about accessibility barriers and the importance of inclusive digital experiences.

For developers, the key lesson is that accessibility should accommodate a range of user needs rather than relying on a single approach.

One of the most common digital accessibility challenges is poorly structured information.

Websites containing lengthy paragraphs, inconsistent headings and complicated sentences may require users to work harder to understand the content.

Developers and content designers may improve readability by organising information into manageable sections.

Useful techniques include keeping paragraphs relatively short, using descriptive headings, placing important information near the beginning of sections and presenting instructions in a logical order.

These changes may benefit users with dyslexia while also making information easier to scan for people using mobile devices or browsing under time constraints.

Typography plays an important role in the reading experience.

Small font sizes, cramped line spacing and decorative typefaces may make content harder to read. Similarly, justified text sometimes creates uneven spaces between words, potentially disrupting reading flow.

Developers should consider readable font sizes, comfortable line spacing, clear visual hierarchy and sufficient contrast between text and background colours.

Although specialised dyslexia-friendly fonts are sometimes promoted as accessibility solutions, research does not establish that one particular font works best for everyone with dyslexia.

Providing users with flexibility is often more useful than enforcing a single typography choice.

Navigation should help users understand where they are, what information is available and how to move between pages.

Unfortunately, some websites rely on complicated menus, ambiguous labels and inconsistent page structures.

These elements may increase cognitive demands and make it difficult for users to locate information efficiently.

Predictable navigation patterns, descriptive button labels and consistent page layouts help reduce unnecessary complexity.

The article A11Y – It's Not Just Colours and Contrast explores how digital accessibility extends beyond visual presentation to include understandable content and predictable interactions.

Designers should remember that an interface may look attractive while still creating unnecessary barriers for users.

Creating more inclusive digital experiences does not necessarily require complicated technology.

Many improvements involve applying established web development practices consistently.

Semantic HTML provides a useful foundation for accessible websites. Elements such as headings, navigation regions, articles and form labels communicate the purpose and structure of content.

Using these elements correctly helps assistive technologies interpret a page while creating a more maintainable structure for developers. Logical heading hierarchies also allow readers to understand how information is organised.

Developers interested in implementing these techniques may explore Semantic HTML and Accessibility Best Practices, which explains how meaningful HTML structures support accessibility.

Clear page architecture is particularly important when building educational platforms, government services and information-heavy applications.

Personalisation offers another opportunity to improve accessibility. Rather than assuming every user prefers the same reading experience, developers may provide options that allow individuals to adjust how content appears.

These features allow users to choose an experience that suits their preferences.

Importantly, accessibility settings should remain straightforward to locate and use.

A customisation feature loses much of its value when users must navigate complicated menus to find it.

Developers frequently work with content designers, technical writers and product teams to create digital experiences.

Collaboration between these disciplines is essential because even technically accessible interfaces may contain confusing language.

Clear instructions, descriptive headings and familiar terminology help users understand what they need to do.

For example, a form displaying the message "Invalid input" provides relatively little guidance.

A more useful message might explain which information needs correcting and provide an example of the expected format.

Similarly, replacing vague button labels such as "Continue" with more descriptive alternatives may help users understand the next action.

Readable content should be treated as part of the overall user experience rather than an afterthought.

Not every person who experiences reading difficulties has dyslexia.

Reading challenges may arise for several reasons, including language differences, educational experiences, attention difficulties or other learning-related factors.

For children, persistent difficulties with recognising words, developing spelling skills or reading fluently may indicate a need for further investigation.

Adults may also recognise longstanding reading difficulties when managing workplace documents, professional training or increasingly complex digital systems.

Developers do not need to diagnose these difficulties. However, understanding that users experience different barriers encourages more thoughtful design decisions.

This is where discussions about professional dyslexia testing services become relevant beyond educational settings.

Understanding the nature of someone's reading difficulties may help educators, families and support professionals identify appropriate learning strategies and digital accommodations.

Professional dyslexia assessments aim to develop a clearer understanding of an individual's literacy-related strengths and difficulties.

Depending on the assessment approach and individual circumstances, this may involve examining reading accuracy, reading fluency, spelling, phonological processing and related learning skills.

Assessment findings may help inform educational support, workplace adjustments and decisions about assistive technologies.

For example, a student who struggles with reading fluency may benefit from access to audio-supported learning materials, while another individual may require different literacy interventions or classroom adjustments.

For families and educators exploring these issues, resources discussing the early identification of reading and literacy challenges offer useful context about professional assessment and individualised learning support.

It is important to distinguish formal assessment from digital screening applications.

A reading application may identify patterns in performance or highlight areas requiring additional support, but those observations should not automatically be interpreted as a diagnosis.

Technology has an important supporting role, although professional interpretation remains necessary when determining the nature of learning difficulties.

Artificial intelligence has introduced new possibilities for improving the accessibility of written information.

AI-powered tools may help users summarise lengthy documents, explain complicated terminology, convert text into speech or reorganise information into manageable sections.

For someone who finds dense written information difficult to process, these features may provide alternative ways to access content.

However, automated systems are not always accurate.

AI-generated summaries may omit important details, misunderstand context or simplify information in ways that change its meaning.

Developers implementing these features should therefore consider transparency, reliability and opportunities for users to access the original information.

Educational technology increasingly incorporates adaptive features designed to respond to individual learning progress.

Reading platforms may adjust difficulty levels, provide audio support or offer additional practice when users encounter challenging material.

Such systems may be especially valuable when they give learners control over how information is presented.

However, personalisation should not rely on simplistic assumptions about learning differences.

Two people with dyslexia may have very different strengths, challenges and preferred strategies.

Effective digital learning experiences should allow for individual variation rather than placing users into rigid categories.

Although technology may provide useful learning support, it should not be presented as a substitute for comprehensive professional assessment.

This distinction matters when developers build educational applications that analyse reading performance or generate recommendations.

An application might identify that a user consistently struggles with certain reading tasks, but interpreting the reasons behind those difficulties requires more than automated performance data.

Educational tools sometimes collect sensitive information about learning performance, academic progress and individual abilities.

Developers should approach this information carefully, using appropriate security measures, transparent data practices and proportionate data collection.

Responsible technology design involves recognising both the opportunities and limitations of automated systems.

Accessibility testing should begin early in the development process. Rather than waiting until a website is complete, teams should review accessibility throughout design, development and quality assurance.

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines provide a useful framework for evaluating digital accessibility.

Developers may review elements such as text resizing, readable instructions, consistent navigation, form feedback and compatibility with assistive technologies.

Automated accessibility tools are valuable for detecting certain technical issues, but they do not identify every usability barrier.

A website might pass automated checks while still containing confusing instructions or unnecessarily complicated workflows.

One of the most valuable ways to understand accessibility challenges is to involve people with relevant lived experiences.

User testing may reveal difficulties that developers would not otherwise anticipate.

For example, participants might identify confusing navigation labels, overwhelming content layouts or instructions that require repeated reading.

Rather than focusing exclusively on how quickly someone completes a task, researchers should also consider whether the experience feels understandable, predictable and manageable.

Testing should involve a variety of participants where possible.

It is also important to avoid assuming that feedback from one person with dyslexia represents the preferences of everyone with the condition. The goal is to identify recurring barriers while respecting individual differences.

Accessibility is not a one-time achievement.

Websites and applications evolve as developers introduce new features, redesign interfaces and publish additional content.

Each change may create new barriers or provide opportunities for improvement.

Development teams should incorporate accessibility into their regular workflows through code reviews, usability testing, design guidelines and ongoing feedback.

Accessibility issues should also be documented and prioritised alongside other technical improvements.

For organisations developing educational technology, these practices become particularly important because users may depend on digital platforms to access essential learning materials.

The relationship between dyslexia and digital accessibility highlights an important principle: good technology should accommodate human differences rather than expecting everyone to interact with information in the same way.

Developers influence how people read, learn, communicate and complete everyday tasks online.

By considering readability, predictable navigation, flexible interfaces and assistive technology compatibility, development teams may create more inclusive experiences.

Understanding dyslexia also encourages greater awareness of the distinction between identifying learning needs and providing digital support.

While discussions around dyslexia testing services primarily concern assessment and educational understanding, they also reinforce the value of recognising that learning differences vary significantly between individuals.

Accessible design does not require developers to become psychologists or learning specialists. It requires curiosity, thoughtful design decisions and a willingness to listen to users whose experiences differ from their own.

As digital platforms become increasingly important in education and everyday life, designing for neurodiversity should be considered a fundamental part of building technology that serves a wider community.

#9824. Hindsight-Driven Development: An Iterative Approach to Building Software With AI

AI scientist, builder, and computer science faculty member.

AI scientist, builder, and computer science faculty member.

AI scientist, builder, and computer science faculty member.

AI makes trying cheaper than guessing, yet spec-driven development still asks you to guess first. Meet Hindsight-Driven Development.

You spend two hours writing a detailed spec for a feature. An AI coding agent builds it in ten minutes. You try it, and within a minute you see what the spec got wrong.

In those same two hours, you could have built it, tried it, thrown away three versions, and kept the fourth.

Specs force us to make our most detailed decisions at the moment we know the least.

For decades, that was a fair trade. Building was expensive, so we paid to describe software first.

AI broke that trade. Yet a popular response to AI coding agents is spec-driven development. Tools like GitHub’s Spec Kit and Amazon’s Kiro have you write and sign off on requirements, a design, and a task list before the agent writes any code. More detail, decided earlier. That gets it backward.

Writing detailed specs for AI agents is waterfall, rebranded for the AI era.

Even when that spec gets edited later, you still decide before you see.

One exception, which I’ll come back to: decide up front whatever is expensive to undo. Build everything else.

Writing a spec means imagining a product that doesn’t exist yet and simulating it all in your head. That takes three kinds of guessing:

No amount of good writing fixes this. Imagination has limits. People don’t know what they want until they see what they don’t want. Yet the spec gets reviewed, approved, and signed off, and the guess gains an authority it never earned.

A spec can be perfectly clear, perfectly consistent, and completely wrong.

If you’ve ever shipped a feature exactly as specified and watched people ignore it, you already know the problem.

We get very good at building what we imagined, and never find out what we actually needed.

Agile admitted part of this problem. But building was still expensive. Three versions of one feature, just to see which felt right? Rarely worth the cost.

So the spec survived as user stories, tickets, and acceptance criteria. Agile shortened the distance between guessing and feedback. You still had to guess first.

Say you’re building a customer-support assistant. Should it ask two questions or five? Suggest a fix early, or wait? Will it feel helpful or pushy? Skip the meeting. Generate one and talk to it.

The first version asks too many questions, forgets what you told it, and jumps to answers too early. You see all three in minutes, and they produce better requirements than anything you’d write in advance.

You might say AI can write the spec in ten minutes too. It can, but only what you already imagine, and the limit was never typing. A faster spec is still a guess.

I call this Hindsight-Driven Development. A spec asks you to decide with foresight, before anything exists. This approach lets you decide with hindsight, after you’ve seen the real thing.

Start with one sentence of intent. Build a rough version, use it, and keep correcting it until it does what you want. The fastest hindsight comes from a real user, so put the rough version in front of one early. The corrections sound like this:

“This workflow is confusing.” “Don’t offer a refund before I’ve finished explaining.” “Show me three different approaches.”

Nobody writes “don’t offer a refund before I’ve finished explaining” into a spec. Everyone says it the first time the bot does it.

The third one matters most: asking for several approaches early stops you from polishing only the first idea.

Predicting what’s right is hard. Recognizing what’s wrong is easy. This approach trades the hard problem for the easy one.

Agile still writes each ticket first. Here, the product writes the next one.

And vibe coding accepts whatever the AI produces and moves on. Hindsight-Driven Development questions every result, corrects it, and keeps every correction as a test or a line in the spec.

Fred Brooks wrote “plan to throw one away” in 1975, then later called that too simple. His better lesson, from 1986: “grow, not build, software.”

Slack began as the in-house chat tool of a team building an online game. The game failed. The tool became the product. The idea is old. What changed is the price.

A prototype used to be a project. Now it’s a prompt.

They do. But a spec written in advance can’t cover a gap nobody knew was there.

Agents drift less from forgetting than from decisions we haven’t made yet.

When the agent guesses wrong, you see it the first time you use the product, and the fix costs minutes. That fix then goes into the tests, and the spec the agent reads next time.

What’s harmful is the spec written first, from foresight, by people asked to imagine what they can’t yet see. Hindsight-Driven Development flips the order: the spec comes last, from what the team has already seen.

Each person corrects the product from their own angle. Only the version you keep goes through code review, and the decisions behind it go into the spec. The ones you throw away cost a few minutes and nothing else.

Every checkable correction becomes an automated test, like “it should remember my order number.” A correction like “this feels confusing” stays a note in the spec until someone decides what better looks like. AI merges it all into one readable spec, flags where people disagree, and asks the team to settle it.

Nobody writes the spec. Everyone shapes it, and AI keeps it whole.

The testable parts stay matched to the product, because a test fails the moment they drift apart. The team aligns around the spec, and the agents read it too, so they stop guessing.

Spec-driven development with extra steps? The document may look the same, but here it records what people saw, not what they imagined.

And the risks no demo reveals, like security holes or failure under heavy load? You don’t guess those either. You inherit the rules others learned the hard way, and test for them. For everything else, workflows, features, and behavior nobody predicted, you discover it by building.

The exception I promised at the start: anything other people build on, like an API another team uses, a customer contract, or anything a regulator requires, is expensive to undo, so agree it up front. That list is short. Most of what a product does sits outside it.

AI now handles much of the slow part: writing the code. The bottleneck becomes deciding what to build, and that’s a job for the whole team: product, engineering, and architecture.

Even architecture works this way. A good design is never written in one go. It starts rough and gets refined, round after round. Until now, all that refining happened on paper. Now the architect refines the working product itself.

The scarce skill now is knowing what’s wrong when you see it.

We spent fifty years getting better at describing software before building it. That made sense when every line took real effort.

That’s no longer true. When a working version of a feature costs minutes, a detailed spec written before a single experiment is premature commitment dressed up as diligence.

For decades, we built with foresight. Now we can build with hindsight.

What’s the biggest thing your spec got wrong that you only saw once the product ran? Tell me in the responses. And if you think I’m wrong, tell me why.

Rethinking Computer Science Education: Why Students Should Build Before They Master Theory

#9823. Your AI agent forgets why. Give it a decision record

Posted on Nov 4 • Originally published at thewebhig.hashnode.dev

You spend a session getting an order form right. One page, not three steps. A review summary before submit. Delivery date where people actually look for it. Then a new prompt regenerates the form, and the agent goes back to a three-step wizard, because nothing told it why you chose otherwise.

The agent kept the code. It did not keep the reasons.

Design Decision Method handles this with step 4 of its workflow: the decision record.

For a choice that would be costly to undo, the method asks you (or your agent) to record:

It also asks you to judge effort in a specific way: compare the effort to read, remember, enter, navigate, and recover, rather than counting clicks or visible elements. A three-step flow has fewer fields per screen. That does not make it less effort if people have to go back to check what they entered on step one.

Say you run a small print shop at example.com, and you ask your agent to build the order form. This is an illustration of how the procedure applies, not a case study or a measured result.

If a source you cite recommends a different pattern for this form, that is where an adaptation line goes, in the same three-part form.

The record also carries a short validation status, because step 6 of the method asks for an honest evidence label on each result: proposed, heuristic review, automated check, manual test, or user research. For this form it might read:

Untested stays untested. The record says so instead of implying the form works.

Next week you ask the agent to add a "rush delivery" option. The following prompt starts from that record. The agent can see the form is one page for a reason, and that the reason is error cost, not taste. It adds the option inside the existing structure instead of reinventing the flow.

A person still checks the result. The method does not measure how many prompts that removes, and whether it saves time has not been measured.

The decision record is proportional. A small change gets a few lines. The repo's design record template is a scaffold, not mandatory overhead. Save the record with the work (as docs/design/.md) when your project keeps design records, or deliver a compact record inline with the change when it does not.

You do not need a record for every edit either. The method is a shared procedure, not mandatory for every small edit. Record the choices you would be annoyed to re-argue.

The decision record is step 4 of six: establish context, choose the visual system, map objects before layout, write a decision record, structure each view, then deliver and validate.

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

#9822. 51 Thanksgiving dessert recipes for a sweet holiday: From cookies to cake — and of course, plenty of pie.

Of course, we had to start with pumpkin pie. This is a rich, well-spiced pie, thanks to a powerful punch of ginger, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, and black pepper. Two hints for a better result: Mix the filling a day in advance to give the spices a chance to bloom, and be sure to remove the pie from the oven while the center is still wobbly, as overcooking it will cause the filling to crack.

Want even more spice in your pumpkin pie? This spice-forward recipe is for you. Using powerful Vietnamese cinnamon — with its more robust flavor profile — gives the pie an even spicier kick. Meanwhile, the filling is super silky-smooth thanks to a few tablespoons of corn syrup mixed in.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

With its retro vibe, this play on classic chiffon pie is noteworthy for its tender rye crust and its bright, light chiffon filling. The zesty cranberry curd and smooth, sweet Swiss meringue play beautifully together. And the gelatin helps the filling set just right so that once refrigerated, the pie can be sliced neatly. Tart and airy, this pie is an excellent counterpoint to a heavy feast.

Shop the recipe: Organic Medium Rye Flour

Intimidated by pie? Don't be! Our guide on How to Bake Pie has everything you need for a successful, stress-free bake.

This double-crusted beauty is generously filled with sweet-tart apples and spiced with cinnamon, nutmeg, and allspice. But the real secret to its flavorful filling is boiled cider, one of our favorite fall ingredients. The sticky tart-sweet syrup adds an extra depth of apple flavor to make this classic pie stand out from the crowd.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Boiled Cider and Instant ClearJel

This unusual method for baking apple pie caught our eye years ago, when a reader sent it via e-mail. But it’s not just a stunt: Baking a pie in a paper grocery bag gives you a beautifully golden brown, perfectly cooked pie, with toothsome yet tender apples (which soften better thanks to the steam trapped by the bag) beneath a streusel topping.

This beloved pie is made much like pumpkin pie, but with mashed sweet potatoes for nuanced flavor and heavy cream for an especially rich custard. Top it with toasted molasses meringue (if you want the pie to be reminiscent of the classic yams and marshmallow dish served at Thanksgiving), or for a simpler option, with freshly whipped cream. (And for a more unconventional version, try this striking Purple Sweet Potato Pie.)

This traditional pie doesn’t use corn syrup — instead, it’s sweetened entirely with brown sugar. The filling is silky smooth, and the pecans on top toast nicely as the pie bakes. Be sure to use high-quality vanilla extract for well-rounded flavor; an optional handful of chopped bittersweet chocolate is a nice addition, too.

If you’re intimidated by pie (or just don’t have time to chill and roll out pie dough) this easier version of pecan pie is for you. A buttery, brown-sugar shortbread crust cradles a gooey honey-sweetened pecan filling. These bars keep well for days, so they’re perfect for baking ahead of Thanksgiving.

This recipe takes classic pecan pie a step further by adding chocolate chips to the filling. The chocolate beautifully complements the pecans' nuttiness; if you choose bittersweet chocolate, it cuts the pie's overall sweetness, allowing all of the flavors to shine more brightly.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Bittersweet Chocolate Chips

Baker's tip: Make and freeze your pie crust early to get ahead on pie prep.

This creamy, decadent pie is positively bursting with maple flavor — be sure to use the best maple syrup you can find and a dash of natural maple flavor to enhance it. One bite of the brûléed maple sugar top and the silky-smooth filling will have you reconsidering your regular rotation of cream pies this Thanksgiving.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar. If you’re only in charge of dessert this year and want to flex a little, this recipe is an impressive (and tasty!) way to do so.

Shop the recipe: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

Mash-up pies are an easy way to please your guests without making multiple pies. This recipe has the best of both worlds: a smooth layer of spiced pumpkin custard plus a rich pecan topping. It’s best made a day ahead so that the flavors can settle, plus there’s one less dish to worry about on Thanksgiving Day.

Shop the recipe: Adjustable Pie Crust Shield

Is there anything cuter than a mini Thanksgiving pie? Filled with a pre-cooked, perfectly spiced filling that’s enhanced with tart boiled cider, these bite-sized treats can be topped with a woven lattice or streusel.

This tart-sweet cake is easy to throw together — made with melted butter, the one-bowl batter is mixed by hand then poured directly over sugared cranberries. If you have cranberries leftover from making sauce or just want to highlight these seasonal berries in other ways, make this cake.

Shop the recipe: Pure Almond Extract and Sparkling Sugar

This stunning pumpkin swirl cake is more than just good looks: It also has a soft, plush texture, thanks to cake flour and sour cream, and a deep pumpkin flavor paired with fragrant vanilla. It starts with one base batter that gets flavored two ways, creating two distinct colors for a striking visual contrast when sliced.

For a more traditional dessert, try this pumpkin-y layer cake. It’s moist and slightly dense from the pumpkin purée, with a tangy cream cheese frosting and sticky caramel glaze.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

In this unabashedly apple-forward apple cake, there are so many apple slices and so little batter, you’ll wonder how (and if) it will hold together. But never fear: As the batter rises in the oven, it knits those slices together to create a tender cake that’s almost creamy and custardy due to the abundance of fruit.

Shop the recipe: Almond Flour and Pure Almond Extract

The pumpkin and pumpkin-friendly spices (cloves, cinnamon, allspice) in this cake meld surprisingly well with the chocolate chips studded throughout. This dark, moist Bundt cake is rich enough to serve unfrosted, and it's just the ticket when you want to serve a dessert that's substantial, yet not too sweet, to finish your Thanksgiving meal. And it keeps well for days, so you can bake it early in the week to help prep ahead.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin-Chocolate Chip Cake

This golden cake is rich, moist, and subtly spiced to complement, rather than overshadow, the natural flavor of sweet potatoes. It also includes a crunchy pecan crust on both the top and bottom, along with a touch of maple syrup in the cake for sweetness. If you’re not a fan of pie, this sweet potato cake just may be the perfect Thanksgiving dessert.

Get the recipe: Pecan-Crusted Sweet Potato Pound Cake

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Tube Pan

With a hidden swirl of coffee-flavored filling, this stunning cake adds an extra dimension to your holiday table. It’s like a pumpkin spice latte in dessert form — and also secretly whole wheat!

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

Wondering how far ahead you can make your cake? Here's how long cake lasts in the fridge and at room temp.

This cake is an old favorite of our readers, with over 300 five-star reviews. It's a recipe where the whole is definitely more than the sum of the parts: The moist, semi-chunky cake is packed with four cups of apples, then spread with the frosting equivalent of brown sugar fudge. The whole thing comes together by hand in one bowl, so it also fits easily into your Thanksgiving prep.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

Shop the recipe: Apple Pie Spice and Vermont Boiled Cider

Why decide between cheesecake and pie when you can have both? This eye-catching two-toned recipe pairs custardy pumpkin pie with creamy cheesecake for a dessert that will satisfy everyone.

For an all-pumpkin Thanksgiving cheesecake, there’s this classic version, which transforms pumpkin pie into a silky, velvety filling. Because it needs to chill before serving, this cheesecake is an excellent candidate for baking a day ahead of Thanksgiving.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cheesecake with Gingersnap Crust

#9814. Building a Private Kubernetes Lab on AWS

For the hands-on side of the Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS) exam, I wanted a lab where I could experiment, break things and start over, and learn the infrastructure layer underneath the cluster too. Hosted practice environments are great for timed exam drills, but not for hardening one cluster over weeks. Local tools like kind or minikube mostly hide the static pod manifests, audit logging and AppArmor profiles the exam asks you to change. Practicing on a real kubeadm cluster is the closest match. kubeadm is the official tool for bootstrapping Kubernetes on your own machines.

The lab also had to stay secure and low-cost. You get full control of the cluster for troubleshooting and hardening, and you can stop the instances when you're not using them to keep costs down.

The lab is a two-node kubeadm cluster on AWS with four properties:

This post covers the design: what the lab looks like and why. The code, the step-by-step build and the reference details live in the repo, tagged for this post: k8s-hardening-lab at ep01. One script builds the lab. Then you bootstrap the cluster yourself, as practice, or let the same script do it with one command.

The edge is the only instance with a public IP, alone in a public subnet. The control plane at 10.0.2.10 and the worker at 10.0.3.11 sit in private subnets with no route from the internet, each subnet in its own availability zone (AZ). Nothing outside can reach the cluster except SSH from your IP to the edge, and the security groups on each instance decide what may pass between them.

Node-to-node peers are security groups, not IP ranges; only the edge's NAT rule uses the private subnets' ranges. The VPC's default security group has no rules.

Traffic flows in two directions, and both pass through the edge:

The edge is a bastion that doubles as a NAT instance for the nodes in the private subnets. The nodes need internet access, and a managed NAT gateway alone costs about $33 a month before data charges. That's more than this whole lab costs at around 40 hours of use a month, and it brings scalability the lab would never use. The edge does the NAT work only while it's running, and it stops when the lab stops.

Each instance sits in its own availability zone, so node-to-node traffic crosses subnets and routing boundaries, which makes NetworkPolicy and CNI troubleshooting realistic. The spread doesn't buy redundancy, though. Losing the edge's AZ takes your SSH access and the cluster's internet with it, and losing the control plane's AZ takes the API server down; real high availability needs duplicates. Cross-AZ traffic costs about $0.01/GB in each direction, which is negligible at lab scale.

A pod has its own network namespace, so it's like a small separate machine inside the node:

With hop limit 1, the token reply can cross one hop, which only gets it as far as the node. Passing it on to the pod would take a second hop, so it's dropped. IMDSv2 is also required, so without a token the pod can't read metadata at all.

With the design in place, the lab is driven from one console. It deploys into your AWS account, with your SSH key and IP; nothing here connects to my environment. Expect about $7–8 a month if you stop it between sessions. You need AWS CLI v2 with credentials, OpenTofu, OpenSSH and curl; the full prerequisites are in the repo. Clone the repo at this post's tag and run the console from the repo root:

After start, you choose how the cluster gets built. start brings up the machines, not Kubernetes. On a new lab, there's no cluster yet, and start ends by listing your two ways to build it:

Either way you end up with the same cluster. A stopped lab keeps its cluster, so later sessions need only start.

The cost breakdown and teardown are covered in infra/README.md. Run stop at the end of every session.

A study cluster should be reliable rather than clever, so the lab accepts a few risks on purpose, and the capstone uses them as the attacker's starting points:

An alternative worth knowing: inbound SSH itself could go entirely, replaced by EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint or SSM Session Manager. But SSM needs an IAM instance profile the lab doesn't have yet, and the nodes would still need the edge for egress, so a combined bastion/NAT keeps the lab to one box.

Once it's built, you have a private Kubernetes lab of your own to troubleshoot, break and rebuild as often as you like. Explore it, and get to know every component and its security implications before the series starts changing them.

The next post, out Tuesday, November 10, scores this fresh cluster against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark with kube-bench and verifies the platform binaries installed here. The repo README maps every post to the part of the lab it builds on.

Follow the series to get it in your feed. Questions or improvements? Drop them in the comments, or open an issue on the repo.

#9813. Four Relationships, One Second Brain: What You Need to Know

Building shared memory for AI agents. Writing Super Second Brain on memory, identity, and human agency.

Building shared memory for AI agents. Writing Super Second Brain on memory, identity, and human agency.

Building shared memory for AI agents. Writing Super Second Brain on memory, identity, and human agency.

Once fidelity becomes high enough, one day you hear something like this.

“On this issue, I think I know you better than you know yourself.”

People do not respond to those words in the same way. Some laugh, some take offense, and some hurt for a long time.

I read that difference along two axes I have used in earlier whitepapers.

The two axes are independent. Some people can bear reality without seeing it well; others see it well but struggle to bear it. That gives us four rooms.

Of the four rooms, ④ looks the most peaceful from the outside. The owner is satisfied, the AI complies, and there is no conflict. The second brain tells its owner what they want to hear with increasing sophistication. The uncomfortable things other people used to say are filtered out by the agent before they arrive.

Room ③ is noisy, but it moves. Pain means something is being seen, and someone who sees can make changes. As experiences of being wrong without falling apart accumulate, ③ moves toward ①.

Room ② is comfortable, and that is where it stops. In terms of the steps in Chapter 4, it has skipped the mirror and gone straight to the representative. The work runs well. But the person that the second brain comes to resemble is less the actual owner than the owner as described by the owner.

I do not want this table used to label people. The same person may be in ① at work and ③ with family. After a week without enough sleep, anyone can slide toward ④. I do, too.

The four rooms do not classify kinds of people. They are a hypothesis about the relationship someone has with a second brain in a particular domain and state. As in my earlier whitepapers, the principle is to look for recurring patterns rather than judge from a single scene.

The same second brain becomes another self for one person, an assistant for another, a mirror for another, and a mechanism for automating self-deception for another.

The two table images reproduce the existing English translation of the author’s original tables. The Korean originals are included in the review package. This essay is part of the ongoing Super Second Brain whitepaper.

If AI Shares Your Memories and Values, Are You Still the Original?

#9811. The Keyboard Habits That Save an Hour a Week in Windows

Posted on Nov 4 • Originally published at tanit365.com

Speed at a keyboard is not about typing faster. It is about never leaving the home row to chase a pointer across the screen. Every trip to the mouse costs a moment of hand travel, a moment of aiming, and a moment of reorientation when you come back to the keys. None of that shows up as a dramatic loss in any single minute, which is exactly why almost nobody fixes it.

The fix is not a giant cheat sheet either. In practice, a small set of keystrokes covers the tasks that office work repeats all day: switching windows, editing a paragraph, sorting a folder, juggling browser tabs. Below are the ones worth the muscle memory, grouped by the job they do rather than by the key they use.

If you only fix one thing, fix how you move between windows.

This is where the biggest daily gain hides, because anyone who writes for a living repeats these motions hundreds of times.

Selecting by word instead of by character is the single habit that changes how fast a draft gets cleaned up. Retyping a badly worded sentence becomes a two-key operation rather than a slow drag of the pointer.

Spreadsheet users get an extra layer. Inside Excel, Ctrl plus an arrow jumps to the edge of the current block of data, and holding Shift as well selects that whole block. On a sheet with a large amount of data, that replaces a long scroll with one keystroke.

Renaming and reshuffling files is the least glamorous part of desk work, and it is fully covered by the keyboard.

Two lesser-known tricks save real time in crowded folders. Typing a letter jumps to the first item beginning with that letter, and typing several letters quickly jumps to the matching name. Holding Ctrl while clicking selects scattered files, while clicking one item and Shift-clicking another grabs the range in between. All of this behaves identically in the Open and Save dialogs inside applications, so the skill carries over everywhere.

Much of the working day now happens in a browser, and the gap between a careful researcher and a drowned one is a handful of keys.

Pinning the tabs you always need keeps them compact and protects them from accidental closure. The browser also remembers several recently closed tabs, not just the most recent one, so pressing Ctrl + Shift + T more than once keeps resurrecting them in reverse order.

A few keystrokes look obscure until the day they rescue you.

Reading a list does not create speed. Deliberate practice in tiny batches does.

Pick a handful of shortcuts, not a wall of them. Match them to whatever you repeat most: if you live in several windows, start with Alt + Tab, the Win + arrow snaps, Ctrl + W and Ctrl + Shift + T, plus F2. Write them on a sticky note beside the monitor, because a physical reminder gets consulted far more often than a page in a bookmark folder. Use them badly for a week, forcing the awkward pause instead of falling back on the mouse. Add the next batch only once the first feels automatic.

Do these work on both Windows 10 and Windows 11? Yes, every shortcut in this guide behaves the same on both versions unless noted otherwise.

Why does Win + V do nothing on my machine? Clipboard history is switched off by default and has to be enabled once in Settings.

Is it worth learning dozens of shortcuts? No. A small set tied to your own repetitive tasks delivers almost all of the benefit, and a long list mostly gets forgotten.

How long before the keys feel natural? Usually about a week of conscious use for a batch of five, after which the motion becomes automatic.

Can I use the same habits outside Windows applications? Most of the editing and browser keys work identically in other desktop applications, so the effort transfers.

What if my screen freezes mid-task? Try the graphics driver restart first; if the machine is still unresponsive, open Task Manager and inspect what is consuming resources.

The full walkthrough, with the complete table of key combinations and the surrounding notes, lives on the original post at tanit365.com.

#9807. Your Context Is the New Moat: Here's Why

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Jack Dorsey says there is no moat anymore. Yet, Palantir is up 668% in five years, Instinct is valued at $10 billion, and Emergent hit $100 million in annualized revenue in eight months. Both can’t be true unless the moat moved.

My bet: it moved to context. The software that wins from here will behave less like a tool and more like a consultant who knows your business deeply: one that tells you what to do, and then does much of it for you.

The cost of building software is collapsing, and agents can now do real work, so everyone is asking. Jack Dorsey (co-founder of Twitter and Square) says there is none; others say distribution is the moat, and Karri Saarinen (Linear CEO) argues that individual taste will always create moats.

https://x.com/jack/status/2114121702515114234

None of them won on the ability to build software. Technically, anyone can release an assistant; Instinct is still worth $10 billion. They won on knowing the customer’s world well enough to do the work, not just support it.

Palantir, built on embedding deeply in how each customer operates, is the clearest case:

The old moats were the ability to build software, owning the customer, and feature breadth with its integrations and switching costs. Now that software can be generated, the first and the last no longer count. The new moats are:

The difference matters. Code can be generated in an afternoon. Context can’t: it builds up from use, decisions, and outcomes, and it compounds.

You can already see the shift. Google Ads’ auto-applied recommendations adjust your campaigns based on your own account’s history, and Shopify Sidekick answers questions and takes actions using your store’s data.

If context is the moat, the practical question is where it lives. The agent world has quietly settled on an almost embarrassingly simple answer: plain Markdown files the agent reads before it acts. That’s the harness: the files, triggers, and tools around a model that decide what it knows and when it moves.

Look at OpenClaw, an open-source personal agent, or gstack, Garry Tan’s open-source Claude Code setup. Each file answers one question:

A chat, a schedule, or an event triggers the agent. It reads those files, then understands, acts, and checks, using tools like a browser, APIs, and code. The result is an answer or completed work.

For an online store, the harness comes down to five files. What makes them work is being specific. Here’s what they might say for a skincare brand:

Now put a harness like this inside a real store. On day one, it simply sets honest expectations: Sam’s first sale will usually take six to seven days.

By month two, it doesn’t wait to be asked. Sam’s Goals.md says returns should be under 4% by December; they’re at 5.8%. So it brings three questions worth asking, each with a “Research this” button.

And when there’s work to do, it says so: nine listings with reduced visibility, fourteen photos to fix, three listings flagged in reviews. Next to each one is a single button: Do it for me.

Start with the five files. Write down your goals, your principles, how your KPIs actually break down, the patterns you’ve already learned, and your users. Write them in plain Markdown, and keep them current.

That’s what turns software from a tool that runs a workflow into something closer to a high-powered consultant with very deep insight into your business: one that tells you what you should be doing, and then does a lot of it on your behalf.

#9805. Dunning Software Is Not an Email Tool With a Retry Button

Ask ten subscription operators what dunning software does and nine will describe email. A failed payment happens, the software sends a sequence of increasingly apologetic messages, and somewhere in there a retry fires. That description is not wrong so much as it is a photograph of the smallest part of the job. The email is the visible tip. Underneath it sits a scheduling problem, a reading problem, and an accounting problem, and the tools worth paying for are the ones that solve all three.

The scheduling problem comes first. A failed card is not one event; it is a type. Insufficient funds clears on a payday rhythm. An expired card never clears on any rhythm, because the number itself is dead. A generic decline is the issuing bank declining to explain itself, and it often succeeds when the retry is presented cleanly a short while later. Software that retries every failure on the same fixed calendar, day one, day three, day seven, is treating three different problems as one, and it pays for the confusion in burned attempts and annoyed customers. The first thing to ask of any tool in this category is whether the decline code changes what happens next.

The reading problem is quieter. Before every retry, something has to re-read the invoice: has the plan changed, has the customer already cancelled, has a manual payment landed through support? Retrying a stale invoice is how double charges are born, and double charges are how a recoverable customer becomes a chargeback and a refund and a story they tell other people. Good dunning reads before it reaches. Bad dunning reaches on a timer and apologizes later.

The accounting problem is the one nobody demos. When money comes back, which attempt gets the credit? If the platform's native retry and the recovery tool both touched the account, vendors will both claim the save, and the merchant ends up paying a percentage on revenue that would have returned on its own. A tool that counts honestly, one door for every recovered dollar, attribution stamped at the moment of recovery, is not a reporting nicety. It is the difference between knowing what you bought and funding someone else's dashboard.

For a fuller map of the category, including how the major approaches differ on exactly these three problems, this explainer on a plain-language map of what dunning software actually does is a solid place to start before any vendor call.

None of this requires the software to be complicated for the merchant. The complexity lives under the hood: the decline taxonomy, the retry calendar, the re-read, the ledger. What the merchant should see is a short list of what failed, what was tried, what came back, and what it cost. When a tool's demo leads with email templates, ask to see those four lists instead. The answers will tell you, in about ten minutes, whether you are looking at dunning software or at an email tool with a retry button.

A small worked example makes the difference concrete. Take a business with 2,000 renewals a month and a first-attempt failure rate of 8 percent: 160 failures. Say roughly half are soft declines, a quarter are expired or replaced cards, and the rest are a mix of generic declines and genuinely dead accounts. A fixed calendar retries all 160 the same way and typically works hardest on exactly the wrong slice — it spends its early, best attempts on the dead-card quarter, which no timing can save, while the insufficient-funds half waits for slots chosen without any reference to payday. A decline-aware schedule inverts that effort: the dead-card slice goes straight to a card-update request and stops consuming attempts, the soft declines are timed to when money actually lands, and the generic declines get one clean, well-presented retry before anyone concludes anything. Same failure queue, same number of total attempts — the recovery differs because the attempts were spent where attempts can work.

That is also the standard Swipe Again's recovery work is built to be judged against: flat-fee, retries woven around the billing platform's own schedule rather than racing it, and a recovered dollar counted exactly once. Judge it the same way you would judge anything else in this category, on your own failure queue, and let the arithmetic argue.

#9803. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

Perfect For: Podcasters, video creators, and content creators needing professional voiceovers in multiple languages.
